title: Agent safety: retries, least privilege, approvals and audit
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Validate-and-retry loops, bounded retries and backoff, constrained tool sets, idempotent actions, human approval for risky steps, append-only audit trails and data residency.
source: Stripe API docs on idempotent requests; AWS Builders Library on retries and backoff; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (excessive agency); Pydantic docs; GDPR overview (EU cross-border transfers)

questions.prompt: Write generate_valid(prompt, max_attempts=3). It calls llm(prompt + error_hint) to get JSON text, validates it with Answer.model_validate_json(text) (Pydantic), and returns the model. On a ValidationError it feeds the error text into the next attempt. After max_attempts failures it raises RuntimeError.
questions.starter:
from pydantic import ValidationError

def generate_valid(prompt, max_attempts=3):
questions.explanation: Other loops pass. The essentials: a hard attempt limit, the validation error fed back, and a deliberate failure path.

questions.prompt: An agent workflow has 4 independent LLM steps. Each step allows the first try plus up to 2 retries. What is the worst-case number of LLM calls for one run?
questions.explanation: Each step can use 1 + 2 = 3 calls, so 4 x 3 = 12. Bounded retries make worst-case cost and latency predictable.

questions.prompt: A client retries a failed API call 4 times with exponential backoff, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and 8 s before the retries (no jitter). How many seconds are spent waiting in total in the worst case?
questions.explanation: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s. In real systems add jitter so many clients do not retry in lockstep, and respect Retry-After headers.

questions.prompt: A client sends POST /payments three times, with the same Idempotency-Key each time, after network timeouts. The server finished processing the first request. How many charges are made?
questions.explanation: The server stores the result under the key and replays it for the duplicates, so the customer is charged once. Without a key the retries could charge three times.

questions.prompt: Write process_payment(key, amount) in Python. RESULTS is a module-level dict. If key is already in RESULTS return the stored result; otherwise call charge(amount), store the outcome under key and return it.

checks.label: stores the result under the key

questions.explanation: In production the key and result live in a database with a unique constraint (or Redis SET NX) so two concurrent requests cannot both charge, and the key is bound to the request payload.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A validate-and-retry loop must have a maximum number of attempts.
questions.reason: An unbounded loop can repeat a failing, paid model call indefinitely.

whys.a: Correct: a hard cap prevents runaway cost and latency, and forces a defined failure path.

questions.explanation: After the cap, fall back (cheaper path, human, error) rather than loop.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Sending the validation error message back to the model on retry improves the chance the next attempt is valid.
questions.reason: Constrained decoding with a JSON schema can guarantee syntactically valid JSON.

whys.a: R is true, but it concerns a different technique.
whys.b: Correct: the error tells the model what to fix (A true). Constrained decoding is a true but separate mechanism, and it guarantees syntax, not semantic correctness.

questions.explanation: Use constrained decoding to cut format errors, and validators for business rules.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Using an idempotency key makes retrying a non-idempotent POST safe.
questions.reason: The client should generate a brand-new key for each retry attempt of the same operation.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false rather than merely unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true, but R is false: the same key must be reused across retries of one operation, otherwise the server sees different operations.

questions.explanation: New operation, new key; same operation retried, same key.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Giving an agent every available tool makes it safer because it can recover from more errors.
questions.reason: Limiting tools to the minimum the task needs reduces the blast radius if the model is manipulated.

whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false (excessive agency is an OWASP LLM risk), R is true.

questions.explanation: Scope tools per task and per user, with read-only variants where possible.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the pattern that handles it.

left.text: A payment call is retried after a network timeout
An auditor asks who approved a refund last month
EU customer data must not leave the EU

right.text: Validate and retry with the error fed back

questions.explanation: Each pattern answers one failure mode: duplicates, irreversibility, accountability, residency, format errors.

questions.prompt: Complete the approval and audit rules.
questions.text: Approval gates should pause {1} steps such as payments or deletions; the audit log should be {2} and record who, what, when and the model {3} used.
questions.explanation: Record the actor, tool, arguments, result, approver, prompt and model versions and a trace id so any action can be reconstructed.

questions.prompt: Which agent action most clearly warrants a human approval step?

options.text: Wiring a large sum to a new beneficiary.
options.why: Right: high-value, hard to reverse, and a common fraud pattern.

options.text: Searching the public product documentation for a customer question.
options.why: Read-only and low impact; approval would add only friction.

options.text: Summarising an internal meeting transcript for the same user who requested it.
options.why: Low risk and reversible; log it, do not gate it.

options.text: Formatting a draft reply into bullet points before the user sends it manually.
options.why: The user already approves by sending it.

questions.explanation: Tier actions by reversibility and impact: auto-allow, allow with logging, require approval, deny. Approval fatigue is real, so gate sparingly.

questions.prompt: EU customer records must stay in the EU, and your agent calls an LLM API. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use region-pinned endpoints and storage, and redact personal data before it leaves the region.
options.why: Right: control where data is processed and stored, and minimise what is sent.

options.text: Send everything to the cheapest global endpoint and rely on a note in the system prompt.
options.why: A prompt cannot control where data is processed.

options.text: Keep the data in the EU but store full prompts and logs in a US analytics tool for debugging.
options.why: Traces and logs are data too and would leave the region.

options.text: Encrypt the connection with TLS and then treat residency as already satisfied by the encryption.
options.why: TLS protects transit, not the location of processing and storage.

questions.explanation: Residency covers storage, processing, logs, backups and subprocessors. Involve legal for cross-border transfer rules.

questions.prompt: Which fields belong in an agent audit-trail entry? Select all that apply.

options.text: Actor or user id, timestamp and trace id.
options.why: Right: who and when, linked to the trace.

options.text: Tool name, arguments, result and approver (if any).
options.why: Right: what was done and who allowed it.

options.text: Model name, model version and prompt version.
options.why: Right: needed to reproduce behaviour later.

options.text: The raw API keys and passwords used by the tools.
options.why: Never log secrets; log which credential id was used instead.

questions.explanation: Make the log append-only or write-once and protect it from the agent itself.

questions.prompt: True or false: schema-constrained decoding guarantees the output is valid JSON but not that its values are correct.

options.why: Correct: constraining tokens enforces structure, not truth or business rules, so you still validate values.
Structure is enforced; semantics are not.

questions.explanation: Keep validators and verifiers for ranges, references and policy.

questions.prompt: True or false: automatically retrying a "send email" tool call after a timeout is always safe.

options.why: The first attempt may have succeeded.
Correct: a timeout does not mean failure, so a blind retry can send duplicates unless the action is idempotent (for example via a message id).

questions.explanation: Make side effects idempotent or check status before retrying.
